title: Duke Nukem Forever
text: I have been a long time fan of the Duke Nukem series and I enjoyed this game like any other first person experience. I found this installment to be a little different from the previous ones but with the technology changes over the insanely long devolopment period of this game, it is fair to say the game will be different. I will say I have a few complaints myself but I enjoyed the game overall. I am glad to see that the game did not receive a large number of DLC to seem like it was a money pit. I thought that the Doctor Who Cloned Me to be rather fitting for the game and it was worth the price I got it for. Okay, back to the base game. The graphics are much better from any previous installments and are pretty impressive for the time of its inception. The UI and AI are fully functional and it provides a challenge but definitely possible. The level design is fairly linear but sometimes allows other approach options and the environment in each level is finely made into a very believable scenario. The control and overall functionality of the game is solid as well as sticking to realistic arsenal choice. Allowing you to carry only two weapons or four if you allow it in the options, you are deciding what weapon is best for each encounter or just to fit your preference. Also, the EGO system makes it similar to Halo's shield system or anything like it. I like that they decided to do something different but I think the old formula of medkits and armor is sufficient. Also, the arsenal is not to far from your arsenal in Duke Nukem 3D but that is not bad. The weapons that are new are the Expander and the Impregnator Gun. Also, the Freeze Ray can't shoot projectiles but only a continuous beam that recharges. Then the Shrink Ray is not a weapon but a story component that changes the combat somewhat since you will be very small. Well, to conclude, I thought this game was a success and I found it very enjoyable and well thought out. Even though it took practically forever to release, the game was good, I would recommend this game to any that wish to play another entry in the series or first person shooter fans.

text: Pixelated Tower Defense done very well! If you like TD games, this one is worth the price of admission.  Charming pixel graphics lend well to the ultraviolence of dart, spike, and push traps, along with all the other fun tricks you'd expect.  The inclusion of a 'rune' system allows you to increase the difficulty on a given level, letting you enjoy it with a fair bit of replayability.  The music is a touch on the flat side, but the sound effects are spot on.  It's quite satisfying to hear a peasant fall to his death after your pusher trap shoves him into a pit. Looking forwards to spending more time on this one, glad I bought it.

title: Dungeon Warfare

The absence of grinding, the fair difficulty make it one of the best games of this kind I played, alongside Gemcraft, the first Defense Grid and Biteality Tower Defense. I liked it, very much.

title: Dungeon Warfare
text: TL;DR: If you like tower defense games, this is an enjoyable TD with a twist. But it has its problems. The graphics and music are well done in the 8-bit era style, nothing to complain here. The gameplay reminded me of Orcs Must Die (or Dungeon Keeper even). You place traps that finish your enemies in various, graphical and delicious ways. In addition to the traps, the levels can have boulders and pits which you can use to your advantage. However, due to the nature of traps, the game lacks some depth. Why? Well, it all boils down to fact that traps have very limited range of operation AND the path is one-way (i.e enemies just run from start to end). Some traps operate on larger area, but the trigger area is usually quite small, like one tile. This means that the path can actually be considered a single line on which you place the traps, and each trap can only affect one short part of the path. And because different traps benefit from proximity, the most efficient solution is usually a small "death alley" where you grind everything to pulp (or toss/drag the in the pits). In many TD games you can use the tower range to your benefit by placing towers in such places that they cover as large area as possible, and areas as early AND as late as possible (to make use of giving your tower more time to work on the enemies). In Dungeon Warfare there is simply no such thing. (Well, there is, but it's more like a special case). Once you realize this, it eats a bit of the experience. Even the most fancy and complex levels can be solved with concentrating on a small space, effectively ignoring much the level. The game does get a bit more complex in the end. And for the record, I haven't completed the game yet, I think I'm at 70% or so. Some random issues: * Start of the game was quite heavily tutorialized, but nothing annoying * Trap tiers and upgrading traps was NOT tutorialized, didn't learn this until later on when wondering what the "tier" means * Going back to old levels to finish the optional gem levels is a bit stupid as all your upgrades make the game super easy (why not limit traps and/or slots per level?) * Music is slightly repetitive... I cannot understand why many indie games have such a short soundtrack. Easy way to add value, folks! Despite all this I'm still enjoying the game quite a bit, and wholeheartedly recommend it. It's just that with some design changes the game could be even better. Maybe for DW2? :)

title: Dungeon Warfare
text: Fun game of tower defense, although not the most innovative. It has some neat extras, such as unlockable traps, and a trap levelling progression. Beat previous levels with added difficulty and gain more experience, which makes future levels easier. All that said, this is truly a TOWER DEFENSE GAME with all the feel of placing towers and zapping the horde of marching toward the door. Don't expect the game play to go much farther than the original gameplay. In fact, it feels like less than the original, because most of the equipment is unlocked through grinding levels. Many hours are spent with the same scant few towers being used over and over, while you try to beat more advanced levels for typical equipment. Yet, for the low cost, there is plenty to like here, and I have spent many hours working out better strategies for the levels, but I also wish it was delivering more of the later game play a bit sooner. I have always had a mischevious spot for dungeon traps, and I had this crazy book in my RPG days filled with all sorts of clever traps for killing characters. This game scratches that itch to a degree, but I kind of wish it hit the mark with a bit more oomph. I think the designers should have realized that there was a lot more fun pushing a mob down a bottomless pit than shooting it a million times with an arrow trap. Ah well!

title: Dungeon Warfare
text: This is how indie game should be Dungeon Warfare is a classic Tower Defense game with 1 small differences. Instead of towers you have traps, a lot of traps, actually. The rules are simple, enemies are approaching, place traps to destroy them. Get gold by killing them and place new traps. Repeat until a level is finished. When you get lvl up and upgrade your traps or get new ones. When new level starts. As i said, it's classic. There were the things I really liked. For example, its really pleasant to see how enemies die :D Nice visual and sound effects. Also, there are a lot of enemies comes, they gather in group and then a group dies... its awesome feeling. There is a lot of everything. There are ground traps, wall traps, hook trap, demon portal which summons units on the path, push trap and etc... so you have unlimited choice of ways to pass every level. You received the experience by passing levels and then you get gems which can be spent on upgrades of towers. It's sad, but they gives small bonuses like -1% cooldown time, but there are a lot of them. I know, some people like systems like this. Also, these upgrades unlocks new upgrade for traps. For example, if you will make 15 upgrade for Spike Trap, it will get 3 upgrades +1 damage /+1 damage and 2 upgrades fro choose, add burning effect on attack twice per activation. There is interesting mechanic for setting difficulty. There are 12 tunes in the game, each rune add an feature to the game (enemies get extra health or you have got only 1 live and etc.). If you take rune to the battle, the game becomes harder, but you will receive increased reward, up to 7 times of basic. So, you can change the difficulty of the game whatever you want with such interesting mechanic. There are also things which I could describe as boring. First of all, the bestiary of enemies is small. I have passed about 15 levels and have met only 7-8 different enemies. There comes an another flow, the design of waves of levels. They are... the same... A bunch of peasants with nobles comes at the first waves. Fast moving thieves com at the 2 or second wave. Then knights with moderate HP and armor appear. At the last wave a lot of Crusaders com, they have large amount of health and heavy armor. So, I after I realized it after ~12 mission, the game become pretty boring for me. Yeah, new traps, units, runes appear... I am an old TD fan, but it wasn't enough for me. Also, this game lacks of strategy. There is no special strategy for different enemies. All traps are good against all enemies. So it's possible to pass the mission without any thinking. I don't think it's a good feature for a strategy game. This game will be interesting for TD fans. People who like sandboxes and games with not strict goals and ways of their achievement will find this game satisfying. But this freedom brings a lack of diversity between missions. Anyway, the game is worth for a try. I recommend it

title: Dungeonmans
text: This is my favorite new rogue-like game. This is a serious rogue-like. The gameplay is nearly identical to T.O.M.E. when it comes to combat. It is very hardcore. Many of your would-be heroes will die during their first quest. Several things set it apart from TOME etc... The sense of humor, which is rather wry and very genre-self-aware. The addition of the Dungeonmans Academy, which is improved by the exploits of your individual chracters, and which in turn improves the lot of your new starting characters and the skill system which allows your character to train any set of class skills, regardless of whatever class you start off with. You start by naming your academy, followed by a brief introduction by the headmaster of the academy. Then you name a hero and pick a starting stat set out of several options, followed by a class and two perks. Maybe your would-be hero's stats aren't up to par - you can dismiss him from the academy and pick another candidate. Then you go out into the world map, like in TOME, looking for monsters (random encounters) and dungeons. During your questing you will find loot - equipment which you can use or melt down for scrap, which you can then use to upgrade your forge, books that teach you skills, or that you can bring back to the academy, rare artifacts that improve the academy, and proof of victory over powerful foes, which you can trade to the trainer for stat increases. Everything you bring back to the academy improves the academy and contributes to the future success of new recruits. Since this is early access, they are still working on balancing issues, and sometimes bugs pop up (I've encountered them mostly while using skill books), but the game plays very well and is very fun.

title: Dungeonmans
text: Dungeonmans is a neat game where you play as an adventurer, explore the realm, likely die horribly, and then - you start a new adventurer in the same world! No, wait, don't go, this is still a rogue-like! You'll find that the dungeons you explored initially will all be procedurally randomized again! Whoo, okay, so! - Dungeonmans is essentially a Rogue-like with a persistent world. You essentially make a seed for a randomly seeded world map, and then spawn your character into it from the Dungeonmans Academy (more on this later). From there you venture out into the world clobbering enemies and likely eventually getting clobbered yourself! When you die, your remains will remain in the level of the world where you died (unless you get to a high enough level, in which case something else happens); and you will have to make a new character to spawn into the world with. Spawning into the world again, you will find that the world map is the same, though there will be some negative effects from your last characters death. Bandits will have set upon the roads and towns, and towns you invested in on prior run(s), dungeons you visited will be randomized to feature new layouts to re-explore, and the remains of your prior adventurer will be around to collect loot and experience from. And that pretty much sums up what this game is all about above. But there is more - and unfortunately, not all that good.... Essentially, if your character gets to a specific level, you can retire your character. Retiring your character you might go and opening an inn, go back to teach further recruits of the dungeonmans academy some learned tricks from your retired character, or just go about wandering. The key problem here though is that is leads to a situation where you'll be doing unfun things like 'farming' characters to level 10 to retire so that you can essentially make better and better dungeonman characters to do things with. Now, as a note, this game does now have an Ironmans mode as of this review, but playing on a single run will have a very generic rogue-like experience that gets away from what the gameplay of dungeomans is really all about - a persistent world. This is one of the odd rogue-likes that I both 'recommend' but give a wary warning about. It is a really interesting example of a rogue-like because it has that persistent world concept, and it is worth experiencing because it is really neat. However, because of the farming factor present, this is also a game I would suggest avoiding if you want a game you could really sink your teeth into and enjoy

title: Dungeons and Dragons: Daggerdale
text: Daggerdale was presented as a hack-n-slash action-RPG in the vein of the "Baldurs Gate Dark Alliance" games that appeared on the XBox and Playstation 2. Those were fairly uninventive RPGs (no party, no significant role-playing or dialogue) but still enjoyable for all that. I was looking forward to more of the same. But Daggerdale doesn't even reach the unimpressive standards of a console RPG. It is a dull and dreary game. The level design is exceedingly linear, and every foot of it looks the same. The music is perhaps the most uninspired I have heard in any recent game, and the "Simlish" speech (doubtlessly used to save on localization costs; why pay for voice-actors when you can just use random grunting in place of speech?) is terrible. The controls are sluggish, the auto-targeting is terrible and the action is poorly paced. Nor is there any redeeming quality in the loot; none of the weapons are in anyway impressive. Story and setting are equally under-whelming. And the savepoints are poorly placed. To top everything else off, the game is buggy; textures didn't show up, the game crashed randomly and too often my on-screen avatar just stopped responding to my controls (my favorite bug is how, in the climatic quicktime event -yes, the game resorts to those, too- my character wasn't even visible on the screen! The only possible saving graces to this game was the inclusion of co-op play... but then, I'm not sure I'd want to subject a friend to this game anyway. The four-hour gameplay, normally a disadvantage, was a god-send since I'm not sure I could have stomached more of this game anyway. Daggerdale sucks. Even at sale it isn't worth the price. Avoid at all costs.
